summary: OneTwoTree is an interactive web platform that tracks rainforest change across Malaysian Borneo (Sarawak and Sabah), Brunei, and Indonesian Kalimantan from 2005 to 2026. Combining NASA SAR radar imagery (Sentinel-1 and NISAR)—which can see through Borneo's heavy cloud cover—with Global Forest Watch tree-cover loss records, the app turns satellite data into a visual story. Users start at the Home Page with a canopy tree in the middle, where the tree trunk represents all of Borneo, the branches represent the four territories, and 19 districts appear as colour-coded leaves based on their forest health. Selecting a location (a leaf) leads to the Annual Ring view, where users can scroll through growth rings from 2005 to 2026 and open the Geospatial Map to inspect district boundaries, radar backscatter, hectare-level deforestation, and recovery trends—making over twenty years of rainforest data easy for the public, researchers, and conservation planners to explore.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

OneTwoTree is an interactive forest monitoring web application that visualizes 22 years (2005–2026) of rainforest change across Borneo—spanning Sarawak and Sabah (Malaysia), Brunei, and Kalimantan (Indonesia). It guides users through three connected views:

  1. Canopy Tree View (Spatial Overview): The home screen models Borneo as a living rainforest tree. The trunk represents the entire island of Borneo, the four main branches represent its four territories (Sarawak, Sabah, Brunei, Kalimantan), and 19 colour-coded leaves represent individual districts/cities graded by forest cover health (Healthy ≥80%, Moderately Healthy 60–80%, At Risk 40–60%, and Severe Deforestation <40%).
  2. Annual Ring View (Time Navigation, 2005–2026): Clicking a region or district transitions into a cross-section of a tree trunk with 22 concentric annual growth rings from 2005 to 2026. Users can scroll their mouse wheel or click individual rings to move forward and backward in time.
  3. Geospatial & Radar Map View (Satellite Evidence): After user selects a year, the user will be redirected to an interactive map cropped to the selected district's official boundary. Users can toggle between Cumulative (2001–Selected Year) and Annual forest loss overlays, switch on NASA SAR Radar Backscatter, and scroll the mouse wheel to watch forest cover, hectare-level deforestation, reforestation rates, and multi-year trend lines update year by year.

How is your project creative?

Most geospatial tools present raw GIS layers and technical charts that feel overwhelming to everyday users. We designed OneTwoTree around a botanical metaphor—using a tree to tell the story of a forest. Moving from the living canopy (where), into the annual tree rings (when), and finally down to satellite and radar imagery (what happened on the ground) turns decades of remote-sensing data into an intuitive, tactile experience.

What tools, coding languages, and datasets did you use?

  • Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite 6, and Tailwind CSS v4. The interactive Canopy Tree and Annual Rings are built with custom procedural SVG geometry (using Catmull-Rom splines and seeded radial noise to generate organic wood grain, bark plates, and growth rings). The geospatial view is powered by MapLibre GL JS (WebGL).
    • NASA OPERA Sentinel-1 RTC & NISAR SAR Pipeline (via NASA GIBS WMTS and Alaska Satellite Facility asf_search) for microwave radar backscatter visualization.
    • Global Forest Watch (GFW) / UMD Tree Cover Loss (v1.11 / v1.13) for dynamic loss tiles and pixel-counted hectare loss statistics using a ≥30% canopy density baseline (Year 2000).
    • GADM v4.1 for official district-level administrative boundaries across Malaysia, Brunei, and Indonesia, paired with Esri World Imagery optical basemaps.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Persistent Equatorial Cloud Cover: Borneo is one of the cloudiest regions on Earth, which frequently blocks traditional optical satellites. Integrating Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR)—which penetrates clouds and smoke day and night—was essential for reliable tropical forest monitoring.
  • Cross-Border Ecosystem Continuity: Borneo's rainforest is shared by three countries, yet data is often siloed by national boundaries. We unified 19 districts across Malaysia, Brunei, and Indonesia into a single consistent baseline.
  • Web Performance & Visual Focus: Official GADM boundary files contain tens of thousands of vertices that lag browser rendering. We built a Python preprocessing script to simplify district MultiPolygons for smooth 60fps WebGL rendering and created an inverted GeoJSON mask so users can focus cleanly on one district at a time.

What benefits does it have, and what is the intended impact?

OneTwoTree bridges the gap between scientific satellite archives and public understanding. By pairing visual storytelling with exact hectare-level loss metrics (ha and km²), the platform helps students, journalists, conservation NGOs, and local land-management planners quickly identify deforestation hotspots, compare annual vs. cumulative canopy loss over a 22-year window, and evaluate whether regional conservation efforts are slowing down forest loss.

Use of SI / AI Tools: AI coding and language assistants (Antigravity / LLMs) were used to assist in generating and debugging React/TypeScript frontend components, SVG procedural ring math, Python data-processing scripts, and editing project documentation.
